name: Lena Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Whitlock's, past the chapel on Hill Street. They've three hundred dairy goats, and the milk goes to a cheese maker in the next valley, plus wheat and field beans on the rest. I start at six with the morning milking, it's a twenty-four-place parlour, so it's on and off, on and off. Then feeding, cleaning, kids in the spring. Two years ago I was a school secretary. Fourteen years of dinner money and head lice letters.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the goats. They're cleverer than people think, and every one of them has a personality. Biscuit, the old lead nanny, opens the gate latch with her lips. What wears me out is that I'm still not good at the kidding. Sue Whitlock can tell a breech from the outside. I'm still learning which end is which, some nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there we are. People get excited about new things and then they settle down. I'd say it to Sue over coffee, and to the women at chapel, who'd mostly agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be glad, honestly. I like learning a thing properly and slowly. I use the AI on my phone now and then, to check a goat question at night when Sue's asleep, and that's all I need it for. A quiet world lets me get good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. I'd sign up for the goat husbandry course the cheese maker runs in February, because I want to do the kidding properly. Money stays as it is, we're careful, we've a good bit put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you check goat questions at night. Does it help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sometimes. It told me once a kid was probably fine when it wasn't. So now I use it to know what to ask Sue in the morning, not to decide anything. That's about right for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Mark think about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mark's an electrician. He says nobody's going to trust a robot to rewire their gran's house. He's fairly calm about it. He's calmer than me about most things.

S0.say: I'd say people get excited about new things and then settle down. I'd say it to Sue over coffee and to the women at chapel, who'd mostly agree.
S0.think: I'd be glad, because I like learning a thing properly and slowly. I use AI now and then for a goat question at night, and that's all I need from it.
S0.do: Carries on as now and signs up for the cheese maker's goat husbandry course in February to learn kidding properly. Keeps the household's savings as they are.
S0.quote: So now I use it to know what to ask Sue in the morning, not to decide anything.
S0.fieldNote: Lena uses AI cautiously, as a way to prepare questions for the person who really knows. She likes slow, proper learning and a quiet world suits her. Her chapel and her calm husband anchor her views.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's up to businesses to do what they need to, and up to families to look after each other through it. I wouldn't want the government stepping in everywhere. I'd say we've been through changes before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the milking parlour is the first thing they'd change. There are already robots for goats, Sue showed me a video. If Whitlock's bought one, I'd be the one moved off milking, because I'm the slowest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a bit and see what the cheese maker's other farms do. If the robots work there, I'd ask Sue to let me learn to run ours, because once a thing's proven I'm happy to learn it. I'd talk to Hannah about apprenticeships, too, because she's thirteen and starting to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when the school changed the office system and I had to learn it all at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did that go, at the school?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly for a month, then fine. I cried in the car park once. Then I was the one teaching the others. I think it'd be like that again, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said families should look after each other. What would that look like for yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mark's brother has a building firm. If I lost hours, I could do his office work, I've done enough of that. And my mum's house money, my share of it, is sitting there for a rainy day.

S1.say: I'd say it's for businesses to do what they need and for families to look after each other through it, not for government to step in everywhere. We've been through changes before.
S1.think: The milking parlour would be the first thing to change, since goat milking robots already exist. If Whitlock's bought one, I'd be moved off milking because I'm the slowest.
S1.do: Waits to see how milking robots work on the cheese maker's other farms, then asks to learn to run Whitlock's. Talks to her daughter Hannah about apprenticeships.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like when the school office system changed all at once.
S1.quote: Badly for a month, then fine. I cried in the car park once. Then I was the one teaching the others.
S1.fieldNote: She expects to be moved first because she's the slowest, and says so plainly. Her past, crying in the car park and then teaching others, shows how she adapts once something is proven. Family is her safety net, through her brother-in-law's firm and her share of her mother's house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'd have to pull together. Families, chapels, neighbours. I wouldn't trust the government to sort it in two years, they can't sort the bin collections. I'd say that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be frightened for Mark more than me. If robots can rewire a house in two years, his whole trade goes, and he's the one who loves his work. I'd be all right, I'd only just started anyway. We've money put by, so it's not about food. It's about what we'd both do with our days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Mark and go through the money properly, which we'd never quite done. I'd overpay the mortgage with some of my mum's money, maybe fifteen thousand. And I'd start something with my hands that people would still buy from a person, goat milk soap, maybe, I've made it for Christmas presents. Sue would sell me milk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A churning feeling. But I'd pray, and I'd get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd start soap. Is that a real plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A hope, mostly. I sold twenty bars at the chapel fair last year. That's not a business. But it's something I could grow while I see which way things go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Hannah and Joel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That God doesn't waste anything, and neither do we. Hannah would roll her eyes. Joel's ten, he'd want to know if the goats would be all right. I'd say Biscuit would outlive us all.

S2.say: I'd say we'd have to pull together as families, chapels and neighbours, because I wouldn't trust government to sort it in two years when they can't sort the bins.
S2.think: I'd be frightened for Mark more than me, because robots that can rewire a house would end his trade and he loves it. It's not about food, since we've savings; it's about what we'd do with our days.
S2.do: Goes through the household finances properly with Mark and overpays the mortgage by about fifteen thousand from her inheritance. Starts making goat milk soap to sell, buying milk from Whitlock's.
S2.feel: Anxious and churning, steadied by prayer and getting on with things.
S2.quote: I sold twenty bars at the chapel fair last year. That's not a business.
S2.fieldNote: The fast timeline shifts her worry onto her husband's trade rather than her own job. She's frank that her soap idea is a hope rather than a plan. She trusts community over government and uses her inheritance to cut debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people to get themselves sorted, if they start now. I'd say families should be talking at the kitchen table, not waiting for a letter from the council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd learn the robot parlour once Whitlock's got one, and I'd probably be the one minding it for a while. That suits me, I'm good at following a system once I know it. After that, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the goat course, then the robot course when the cheese maker's farms have them. I'd grow the soap slowly, a market stall once a month. And I'd want Mark to look at the solar and battery work, because that's newer and he says it's busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. But it's the kind you can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're good at following a system. Is that a strength or a worry here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. If the system is a robot, it might not need a follower for long. But I'd rather be the one who knows how it works than the one standing outside watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI more in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, once Sue does. She's started using it for the cheese orders. If it's good enough for her, I'd learn it properly.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for people to sort themselves out if they start now, talking at the kitchen table instead of waiting for a letter from the council.
S3.think: In five years I'd learn the robot parlour and probably mind it for a while, which suits me because I follow a system well. After that, I don't know.
S3.do: Takes the goat course and then the robot course once the cheese maker's farms have robots. Grows the soap into a monthly market stall and encourages Mark towards solar and battery work.
S3.quote: But I'd rather be the one who knows how it works than the one standing outside watching.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets her follow her usual pattern of learning once something is proven. She sees her talent for following systems as both a strength and a risk. She'd adopt AI more once her employer does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time. Plenty of time for families to plan and for young ones to learn a trade. I'd say don't panic, plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'm fifty-three, the kids are grown or nearly, and we've the house close to done. I'd be fine. I'd just want Hannah and Joel to choose well. That's where the worry goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on at Whitlock's, get good at the goats. Learn the robots when they're proven. I'd talk with Hannah about apprenticeships properly, maybe something with care or nursing, where people want people. Joel would go into Mark's trade, I think, if there's still a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit wistful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said wistful. About what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About Biscuit and the others, if I'm honest. A farm with goats and no people in the parlour. I'd miss the noise of it. I'd hope Whitlock's would keep a person on for the kidding, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time change anything with the money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep saving and probably help Hannah with her training costs. I'd not go spending on anything big. Mark wants a new van, he can have it in year three.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time, enough for families to plan and young ones to learn a trade. I'd tell people not to panic but to plan.
S4.think: At fifty-three, with the kids nearly grown and the house close to paid, I'd be fine. The worry goes to Hannah and Joel choosing well.
S4.do: Stays at Whitlock's, gets good with the goats and learns the robots once proven. Talks with Hannah about care or nursing apprenticeships and keeps saving to help with her training costs.
S4.quote: A farm with goats and no people in the parlour. I'd miss the noise of it.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years calms her, and her focus moves to her children's choices. Her sadness is about the animals and the parlour's noise, not money. She plans to help her daughter with training costs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because of Mark. What would help is apprenticeships for grown-ups, not just teenagers, so a man of forty-five could learn a new trade properly while still earning. And fewer forms for little businesses like the soap.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the animals, maybe. Biscuit opens gates. A robot might milk her, but it won't laugh when she gets out. Somebody should still be there to laugh.

headlineQuote: A robot might milk her, but it won't laugh when she gets out. Somebody should still be there to laugh.
portrait: Lena Abbott is 43, a former school secretary two years into work on a goat dairy and arable farm, where she's still learning to handle kidding. She's a chapel-goer who trusts families and community more than government, and she uses AI carefully, mainly to work out what to ask her boss. She follows new things once they're proven, as she did when her school's office system changed. Her worst fear, in AGI by 2028, is for her electrician husband's trade rather than her own job, and with more time her attention turns to her goats, her soap-making hopes and her children's choices.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, mainly because of what it would do to her husband's electrical trade.
whatWouldHelp: Apprenticeships for grown-ups who can keep earning while they learn a new trade, and fewer forms for small businesses.
